title: I posted a sprite pipeline here 10 days ago. Then I made a whole game with it to see if it holds up
author: Head-Language4082
selftext:
Ten days ago I posted about making game sprites by going through 3D instead of asking an image model for frames directly. I was not sure it would survive a real game, so I made a small one to find out: a girl with an umbrella puts out a burning forest. The video is the game running, rounds 1 to 10.

Why 3D at all: when I asked an image model for a walk cycle, I got a character whose face changed between frames and who always had the same leg in front. So now one illustration becomes a 3D model, the model gets a rig and a walk, it is rendered at the game's isometric camera in each facing, and the image model only redraws each frame over that render. The body, the angle and the motion come from the 3D; the image model only does the drawing. She walks, stands and swings in four facings and stays the same person, which was the part I was worried about.

What I did not expect was how much the 3D kept being useful after the art was done. The shadows on the ground are baked from each prop's model, so a tree's shadow is dark by the trunk and pale under the crown. The crowns sway in the wind in clumps cut from the model, a pixel at a time, with no hand-drawn frames. And where a fireball breaks on cover is the model sliced at the fireball's height, so a trunk stops it and the leaves above do not. None of that was planned; each one came up while making the game.

Plenty went wrong. Image models still draw a wrong hand now and then. At small sizes the umbrella came back in four different yellows across her facings, and prompting did not fix it - I ended up reading the object's colours off the 3D render and repainting them in code. And the day I put the game online it would not start on an iPhone: Safari could not play my .ogg sounds, and it read a greyscale PNG I used as a data map back with different pixel values than every other browser. Each took an afternoon to find.

Everything is AI-made: GPT image models for the drawing, Tripo for the 3D, Suno for the music, Claude for the code.

Has anyone else here kept the 3D around after generating the art? I would like to know what you used it for.

The game, if you want to try it: [https://stevebaek0112.itch.io/rain-girl](https://stevebaek0112.itch.io/rain-girl)

The pipeline is open source: [https://github.com/Sunghwan0112/spritecast](https://github.com/Sunghwan0112/spritecast)

comments.author: Cosmonan
comments.body: Don't forget to add ambient occlusion so your sprites don't look detached from the world

replies.author: Head-Language4082
replies.body: Thanks. The props and the girl have ground shadows baked from their 3D models, but the fire monsters only get a very faint contact shadow, since they're light sources. Looking at it again, they do float a bit.

replies.author: Head-Language4082
replies.body:
Update: you were right, so I fixed it. The fire monsters now have a real contact shadow, the girl's and the props' shadows are about 1.5x deeper, and the night is a touch brighter so they read. Before/after in the GIF.

What I learned: shadows baked from the 3D light are physically right but too quiet for pixel art, which needs things said a bit louder. I've made 1.5x the default for pixel sprites in the SpriteCast skill too, so this came straight out of your comment. Thanks.

https://reddit.com/link/1y0kxlf/video/dt0m63spfo2i1/player

comments.author: Ok-Investment4414
comments.body: swings like she got a bad back...needs a chiropract

replies.author: Head-Language4082
replies.body: Ha, fair. She’s been carrying a full umbrella of water for ten rounds. The swing is a 3D animation rendered into sprites, so I can swap in a better one and re-render without redrawing by hand. A bigger wind-up is on the list.

comments.author: Head-Language4082
comments.body:
https://i.redd.it/d7tp9f9gho2i1.png

Update: the shadows got a pass. The fire monsters now have a contact shadow under them, the girl's and the props' shadows are about 1.5x deeper, and the night is a touch brighter. Things should sit on the ground now instead of floating over it.

What I took from it: shadows baked from the 3D light are physically right but too quiet for pixel art. It wants them said a bit louder.

Tip: fireballs break on rocks and tree trunks, but your water goes over the top. Fight from behind cover.

comments.author: riccioverde11
comments.body: I spare you the time, it doesn't

replies.author: Head-Language4082
replies.body: Fair enough. To be honest, the game was built as a test bed for the pipeline, not as a polished release, one monster, only four directions. SpriteCast can render eight directions, and nothing stops you from adding more monsters, actions or props. I'm sure people who use it well will get much better results than I did.
